lead: A one-kilogram block of ice left in a warm room warms, then sits at 0 °C while it melts, warms again, then sits at 100 °C while it boils. The same heat does different jobs: raising temperature, pulling a phase apart and, when a reaction runs, rearranging chemical bonds. Boiler design, refrigeration and every reactor energy balance need these kept separate.
prereq: You need: enthalpy and the first law from the basic concepts of thermodynamics, and Cp from ideal-gas processes.

blocks.text: Sensible heat is heat that changes the temperature of a substance. No phase change, no reaction. A thermometer shows the change, so the heat is called sensible.
Q = ∫ n C<sub>p</sub> dT, from T<sub>1</sub> to T<sub>2</sub>
blocks.where: Q is heat added (kJ); n is amount of substance (mol); C<sub>p</sub> is molar heat capacity at constant pressure (kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); T<sub>1</sub> and T<sub>2</sub> are the initial and final absolute temperatures (K).

blocks.text: When Cp is nearly constant over the range, the integral collapses to Q = n Cp (T₂ − T₁). Working in kilograms gives Q = m cp ΔT, where m is mass (kg), cp is specific heat capacity (kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹), and ΔT is the temperature change (K or °C — the size is the same).

C<sub>p</sub> of a gas climbs with temperature, so one number is only an average over the band. Use a mean C<sub>p</sub>, or fit C<sub>p</sub> = a + bT + cT² (data books list a, b and c for each gas) and integrate term by term: Q = n[a(T<sub>2</sub> − T<sub>1</sub>) + (b/2)(T<sub>2</sub>² − T<sub>1</sub>²) + (c/3)(T<sub>2</sub>³ − T<sub>1</sub>³)].
Sign rule: Q is positive when heat enters the system. A 1 kg aluminium pot heated from 30 °C to 120 °C takes in 1 × 0.90 × 90 = 81 kJ before the food inside warms.

sections.h3: Latent heat moves the molecules apart

blocks.text: Latent heat is heat that changes the phase of a substance at constant temperature and constant pressure. Nothing warms; the attraction between molecules gives way.
Q = m Δh
blocks.where: m is mass (kg); Δh is the specific latent heat (kJ kg⁻¹): Δh<sub>fus</sub> for melting, Δh<sub>vap</sub> for boiling, Δh<sub>sub</sub> for solid to vapour.

blocks.text: At 1 atm, for water, Δh<sub>fus</sub> = 334 kJ/kg at 0 °C and Δh<sub>vap</sub> = 2260 kJ/kg at 100 °C. Each pair belongs to its own pressure; at another pressure both the value and the transition temperature change.

The 2260 kJ/kg does two jobs. About 170 kJ/kg pushes the atmosphere aside as the vapour expands: PΔv = 101.3 kPa × (1.673 − 0.001) m³/kg = 169 kJ/kg, the PΔV part of ΔH = ΔU + PΔV. The rest raises internal energy by breaking hydrogen bonds. That is also why a steam burn at 100 °C is far worse than a water burn at 100 °C: condensing steam gives up its 2260 kJ/kg on the skin first.

sections.h3: Heat of reaction: constant pressure and constant volume

blocks.text: A reaction swaps one set of bonds for another, and the enthalpy difference leaves as heat. Run it in an open beaker at constant pressure and the measured heat is Qp = ΔH<sub>rxn</sub>. Run it in a sealed bomb at constant volume and the measured heat is Qv = ΔU<sub>rxn</sub>.
ΔH = ΔU + Δn<sub>g</sub> R T
blocks.where: Δn<sub>g</sub> is moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is in K. Only gases are counted.

blocks.text: The standard heat of formation ΔH°<sub>f</sub> is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound forms from its elements in their standard states, at 1 bar and a stated temperature, almost always 298.15 K. Elements in their standard state have ΔH°<sub>f</sub> = 0 by definition: O₂ gas, N₂ gas, and carbon as graphite, not diamond.
ΔH°rxn = Σ ν ΔH°f(products) − Σ ν ΔH°f(reactants)
blocks.where: ν are the stoichiometric coefficients from the balanced equation.

blocks.text: The heat of combustion follows the same pattern: 1 mol of fuel burns completely to CO₂ gas and liquid water. It is easy to measure, so tables are full of it.
Hess's law: enthalpy is a state function, so a reaction run in several steps releases the same total heat as one step. Add the ΔH of the steps, flipping the sign of any step you run backwards.

sections.h3: Kirchhoff's law: heats of reaction at other temperatures

blocks.text: Heats of reaction are tabulated at 298 K, but plants run hotter. Kirchhoff's law carries ΔH from one temperature to another.
ΔCp = Σ ν Cp(products) − Σ ν Cp(reactants)
blocks.where: ΔCp is the heat capacity change per mole of reaction (kJ mol⁻¹ K⁻¹), using the same ν as the balanced equation.

blocks.text: ΔH<sub>T2</sub> = ΔH<sub>T1</sub> + ΔCp (T2 − T1)
blocks.where: valid when ΔCp is constant; otherwise use ΔH<sub>T2</sub> = ΔH<sub>T1</sub> + ∫ΔCp dT from T1 to T2.

blocks.text: The reason: products and reactants warm by different amounts, so the enthalpy gap between them drifts with temperature. Kirchhoff's law is sensible heat applied to that gap.

Real fluids need real data: enthalpies along the ice-to-steam path come from steam tables, not constant c<sub>p</sub>, and gases far from ideal need a residual-enthalpy term, which comes later with property relations.

spec.aria: Enthalpy from 0 to 3200 kilojoules per kilogram against temperature from minus 20 to 130 degrees Celsius. The path rises gently from minus 10 to 0 degrees by 20.9, jumps straight up by 334 at 0 degrees, slopes up by 418 to 100 degrees, jumps straight up by 2260 at 100 degrees, and ends with a short slope of 40.2 to 120 degrees, a total of 3073.1.

examples.question: 1 kg of ice at −10 °C is heated at 1 atm until it becomes steam at 120 °C. Take cp,ice = 2.09 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, Δh<sub>fus</sub> = 334 kJ/kg, cp,water = 4.18 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, Δh<sub>vap</sub> = 2260 kJ/kg, cp,steam = 2.01 kJ kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. Find the total heat supplied and the percentage of it that is latent heat.
steps: warm the ice from −10 °C to 0 °C: Q1 = m cp ΔT = 1 × 2.09 × 10 = 20.9 kJ.
melt the ice at 0 °C: Q2 = m Δh<sub>fus</sub> = 1 × 334 = 334 kJ. Temperature stays at 0 °C.
warm the liquid water from 0 °C to 100 °C: Q3 = 1 × 4.18 × 100 = 418 kJ.
boil the water at 100 °C: Q4 = 1 × 2260 = 2260 kJ. Temperature stays at 100 °C.
superheat the steam from 100 °C to 120 °C: Q5 = 1 × 2.01 × 20 = 40.2 kJ.
add the five parts: Q<sub>total</sub> = 20.9 + 334 + 418 + 2260 + 40.2 = 3073.1 kJ.
examples.answer: The total heat is 3073.1 kJ per kg, of which 2594 kJ (84.4 %) is latent heat.

examples.question: For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), find ΔH°<sub>298</sub> and ΔU°<sub>298</sub>, then ΔH at 700 K by Kirchhoff's law. Data: ΔH°<sub>f</sub>(NH₃, g) = −46.11 kJ/mol; C<sub>p</sub> (J/(mol·K), taken constant): NH₃ 35.06, N₂ 29.12, H₂ 28.82.
steps: ΔH°<sub>298</sub> = 2(−46.11) − [0 + 3(0)] = −92.22 kJ per mole of reaction (elements have ΔH°<sub>f</sub> = 0).

Sign check: ΔC<sub>p</sub> < 0, so the reaction becomes more exothermic on heating, as found. The C<sub>p</sub> of NH₃ rises faster with T than those of N₂ and H₂, so |ΔC<sub>p</sub>| shrinks on heating and a polynomial C<sub>p</sub> gives a smaller shift than this constant-C<sub>p</sub> estimate.
examples.answer: ΔH°<sub>298</sub> = −92.22 kJ and ΔU°<sub>298</sub> = −87.26 kJ per mole of reaction; with constant C<sub>p</sub>, ΔH<sub>700</sub> ≈ −110.5 kJ.

traps: Adding latent heat at the wrong temperature: fusion belongs at 0 °C and vaporization at 100 °C only at 1 atm. At 2 atm the boiling term sits near 120 °C with a smaller Δh<sub>vap</sub>.
Forgetting the sensible heat on one side of a phase change — the ice warming to 0 °C, or the steam superheating after 100 °C.
Sign of ΔH: exothermic is negative, endothermic is positive. Write the sign in every line, not just the last one.
Using Qp = ΔH when the vessel is sealed: at constant volume the measured heat is ΔU, and ΔH = ΔU + Δn<sub>g</sub> RT with T in kelvin and only gases counted in Δn<sub>g</sub>.

quiz.q: Define sensible heat and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: Heat that changes the temperature of a substance without a phase change or a reaction; measured in joules (J).

quiz.q: Why does the temperature stay at 100 °C while water boils, even though heat keeps entering?
quiz.a: The energy goes into pulling molecules apart against their attraction — potential energy — not into the average kinetic energy that a thermometer reads.

quiz.q: A gas-phase reaction has ΔU = −50.0 kJ at 400 K with Δn<sub>g</sub> = −2. Find ΔH.
Why does ΔH<sub>rxn</sub> change with temperature at all? Where does the change come from?
quiz.a: Products and reactants have different heat capacities, so they warm by different amounts and the enthalpy gap between them changes with temperature at the rate ΔC<sub>p</sub> (Kirchhoff's law). For ammonia synthesis ΔC<sub>p</sub> = −45.46 J/K, so ΔH moves from −92.22 kJ at 298 K to about −110.5 kJ at 700 K.

quiz.q: A student heating ice from −10 °C adds 2260 kJ/kg as the first step. Explain the error and give the correct order of steps.
quiz.a: 2260 kJ/kg is the latent heat of vaporization, valid at 100 °C, not for ice at −10 °C. Correct order: sensible heat of ice to 0 °C, fusion at 0 °C, sensible heat of water to 100 °C, vaporization at 100 °C, then sensible heat of steam.

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant heat balances use steam tables and residual enthalpies instead of constant c<sub>p</sub>, and pinch analysis pairs hot and cold streams so that utility steam is minimised. Heats of formation of unstable compounds are now computed by quantum-chemical methods. Search for enthalpy of formation databases and pinch analysis.
